title: Sales materials
brief_markdown:
Everything in this chapter is the Module 2 narrative recast into formats a prospect can consume without you in the room. If the narrative is shaky, materials only make the shakiness prettier. If it holds, materials let it travel: into a LinkedIn note, a 20-minute call, a two-minute video, an email that gets forwarded to the person who actually signs.

### Speed beats polish
The founder trap is believing nothing can go in front of a prospect until it looks like a funded company's website. At this stage the opposite is true. The loop that matters: hear an objection from an agency owner on Tuesday, have a slide that answers it by Wednesday. Ten rough screen recordings of the real Myda product, one per feature, will book more calls than one animated explainer that ships in March. When "perfect" and "good enough to persuade" conflict, choose speed. Steal your pitch deck's colours and logo for a template and move on. Design is never a gate.

### The deck
Slides first, before demo scripts and videos, because one deck does everything: you talk over it live, you send it afterwards, you cut three slides out for a LinkedIn message, you record a video over it, you screenshot one slide to make a point in a reply. And it is what a Head of E-commerce expects to receive. Technical founders want to skip to the demo. A demo without the deck is a feature tour with no reason to care; the deck sets up the problem so the demo lands.

**Structure follows the narrative.** The minimum deck is one slide per narrative question: problem, who has it, cost, how it is solved today and why that fails, what changed, how Myda works, proof, price. Eight bullet slides is a legitimate v1. Then "zoom in" where conversations demand it: the single solution slide becomes one slide per value bucket (say *faster feedback rounds*, *creators who improve video over video*, *winners you can reproduce*), and later each bucket gets screenshots. Keep the summary versions; you choose the zoom level per audience.

Section by section, with Myda in mind:

- **Problem and who has it.** Start here so a prospect who does not have the problem can tell you in minute one. Add validators: a TikTok Shop stat on creator-video volume, one line from a beta tester, a screenshot of a 14-message feedback thread in someone's Slack. "Many people agree this hurts" is a stronger claim than "this hurts".
- **Cost.** Put units on it. Hours of review per content person per week, the freelance fee for a video that misses the brief, GMV concentrated in two of the forty videos that shipped. Make it a formula the prospect can run on their own account: *creators × videos per month × minutes of feedback per video*.
- **Existing solutions.** Normally you do not raise competitors. The exception is when everyone in the room already uses the alternative, and for Myda that is the case: every agency has tried ChatGPT for scripts, every brand has a UGC agency or a Slack channel full of feedback. One bucket slide (nothing / process / agency / AI tool) with the honest strength and the gap of each. Granting the strength is what earns the right to name the gap.
- **What changed.** This slide is a comprehension check as much as content. A one-line timeline (brand-made ads → affiliate creators → TikTok Shop turns creator video into the sales channel → models can now watch a video against a brief) lets you pause and see whether Marcus is nodding or doing email. The worst meeting is the one where he never understood and politely disappeared.
- **How it works.** One diagram before any feature: brief in, creator video in, 1:1 feedback out through Discord or email, loop repeats. Anchor it to something known: "a creative director who reviews every creator video within the hour".
- **Proof.** Quantitative first, in metrics they already track, bucketed by value prop: minutes of feedback per video before and after, hook rate on round-two videos, approved videos per week. No numbers yet? Then the slide says what the beta measures, not an invented figure. Qualitative second: write the testimonial for your beta tester and ask them to approve it. Logos: show them live, do not email them yet.
- **Why this will be easy.** Sophisticated buyers have been burned by onboarding. For Marcus, "I'm not switching workflows mid-Q4" is this slide: his creators already live in Discord, feedback arrives where they are, nothing in his stack changes.
- **Pricing.** One slide, one option, the one from Module 2. Variants live in your head, not on the slide.
- **Appendix.** Anything asked twice gets a slide: "how is this different from ChatGPT?", "do you handle Spark Ads?", "who sees our creators' videos?". Thirty minutes once saves you fumbling the answer twenty times.

**Two decks.** The one you present (plus the appendix you jump into) and the much shorter one you send afterwards: a reminder for the person who was there and a teaser for the manager it gets forwarded to. Send it through something that shows opens and time per slide; a minute on the pricing slide is a buying signal. Keep one master deck as the repository and fork a copy for every version you send, so nothing is ever lost.

**Customisation.** The highest-leverage move in the chapter: put the prospect inside the materials. Their TikTok Shop creators' videos are public. Drop a frame of one onto the problem slide. Run Myda feedback on three of them before the call and open the demo with it. Generic materials look like a vendor demo; customised ones look like a diagnosis.

### Outreach templates
Emails and LinkedIn messages are the narrative compressed to drive one outcome: a live 20-minute conversation. They do not sell the product; they earn the call. Rules that hold for Myda:

- Be specific about the pain and show you checked: "I watched six of your creators' videos for {brand}; four open with the same hook" beats "content is hard".
- The prospect's point of view, always. Not what Myda does, what changes for them.
- Plain text, peer tone, no marketing images, no jargon. Anything that looks designed reads as spam.
- One click target (a two-minute video or a slide screenshot) so you see who is interested before they reply, plus a link to the site.
- One call to action with a concrete ask: "20 minutes Tuesday or Thursday?"
- Build them as a series from day one: message one is short with the biggest number, two goes deeper on one value bucket, three on another, four is a beta-tester story. Same ask every time.

**Warm intro.** When a 2nd-degree LinkedIn contact knows the target, do not ask for an introduction. Send the introducer a forwardable email written for the target, with a line on why you picked them and something scarce (a closed beta, three spots left). The introducer passes it on with one sentence of endorsement; the target opts in by replying to you. Track the open; if nothing in a week, treat the target as cold outreach with warm context.

**Phone and voicemail.** Not a script to read, a bullet list to land in 30 to 90 seconds: who you are, why them specifically, the problem in their words, the ask. Pre-write the branches: interested (offer two slots), a follow-up question (defer it to the demo), not interested (state the cost of waiting, once), "is it free?" (no, and here is the return; price detail belongs in the call), "is it like ChatGPT / our agency?" (yes, and here is the difference the demo will show), hard no (say you will follow up next month, then do). Voicemail is an audio email: pair it with a real email in the same hour.

### Demo script
Module 7 covers delivery; write the skeleton now. Order the buckets by importance to the buyer, not by product flow, because demos get cut short. Tell the story of a workday: creator uploads, brief is checked, feedback goes out, round two comes back better. Pause after each bucket. Research before you ask: not "what is your hardest brief?" but "you ship about forty creator videos a month for {brand}; here is what feedback on three of them looks like". Product requests that make the demo easier (paste a TikTok link, get feedback live) are revenue features even if no customer asks for them.

### Video
A two-to-five-minute overview recorded over the deck with Loom or QuickTime, ums included, posted where it plays on a phone. Its job is not to sell Myda; it is to earn the call. Put it in every template. The polished explainer can come later and must not block the rough one.

### Everything else
One-pagers, webinars, case-study PDFs: later. When a prospect asks "do you have a one-pager?", find the question under the question; usually the first eight slides of the send-deck already answer it. The one piece worth building on demand is the customised one: a screenshot of Myda's feedback on one of their creator's videos, made in sixty seconds, beats any generic PDF. Treat every piece of collateral as a feature: it costs time to build and maintain, so weigh how often it will be used against what it earns.

build.spec_markdown:
Produce {{company}}'s sales-materials pack, section by section, in this order. Work one question at a time; record each section with update_artifact as soon as it is good enough, then move to the next. Pull the problem, who has it, cost, alternatives, what changed and the price from the company artifact's Narrative and Pricing sections; do not re-litigate them here.

1. **Deck outline.** Main deck of 10 to 14 slides, one line per slide: headline (a sentence the prospect would agree with, not a topic), two or three bullets, the narrative question it answers, the visual or proof it needs and whether that exists today (`TODO: measure in beta` if not). Mandatory: problem + validators, who has it, cost formula, existing-solutions bucket, what-changed timeline, how-it-works diagram, proof, why this will be easy, pricing. Then an appendix list seeded with every objection Dana and Marcus raised in Modules 1 and 2 and in the CRM log.
2. **Send-deck.** Which 6 to 8 slides go in the version emailed after a call, and the one-sentence covering note.
3. **Outreach templates**, each with a subject or first line, body, one click target and one call to action: (a) LinkedIn connection note, 300 characters max, the one both founders will actually send twenty times a day; (b) LinkedIn follow-up once accepted; (c) cold email, 150 words max; (d) forwardable warm-intro email plus the two-line note to the introducer; (e) a four-step drip outline naming which value bucket each step leads with.
4. **Phone script.** 60 to 90 seconds of bullets, then the branches: interested, follow-up question, not interested, "is it free?", "is it like ChatGPT / our agency?", hard no. Plus a 20-second voicemail.
5. **Demo skeleton.** Three value buckets ranked by importance to the buyer, the workday story, the pause points, and the pre-call customisation checklist (prospect's TikTok Shop brand, three creator videos pulled, what {{company}}'s feedback on them said).
6. **FAQ / appendix answers.** Two to three sentences each, granting the alternative its strength before naming the gap: ChatGPT, UGC agency, is it free, show me the data, who else uses this, not switching mid-Q4, who sees our creators' videos.
7. **Overview video.** A two-minute script outline over the send-deck, plus the recording to-do with an owner and a date.

Standards to enforce on every section: each template names a TikTok Shop pain in the prospect's words and would make a stranger like Dana or Marcus say "that's me"; each message has exactly one call to action; no jargon, no marketing images; no number appears in proof or templates that {{company}} has not measured (write `TODO: measure in beta` instead). Push back on generic copy ("AI-powered feedback platform") and on templates that pitch the product instead of earning the call. Mark the artifact done only when all seven sections exist and the LinkedIn note is one both founders would send tomorrow.

drill.time_limit: 6 exchanges, about 15 minutes; every seller email under 150 words
drill.scenario: Two days after the Austin event (Module 2), Marcus emails: before he puts anything in front of his TikTok Shop manager he wants something he can forward. Reply with the send-deck and overview video from the materials pack, describe what you attach the way a real email would (slide titles, video length), and drive to a 30-minute customised demo with him and his TikTok Shop manager. He tests the materials by email: 'how is this different from my team using ChatGPT?', 'show me the data', 'what does it cost?', 'we have an agency for this'. He reads on his phone, so anything over 150 words gets skimmed. Answer only what earns the meeting; the rest belongs in the demo.
drill.buyer_opening:
Good to meet you in Austin. Before I put anything in front of my TikTok Shop manager I need something I can forward. Send me what you've got.

Marcus

rows.criterion: Opened by reminding Marcus of the hallway conversation in his own words (the problem as he stated it), not with a re-pitch
Sent the right thing: a short send-deck built for forwarding, slide titles named, not the full master deck
Included one click target (overview video or demo link) plus a link to the site, with a reason to click
Wrote from Marcus's point of view in plain peer language: every seller email under 150 words, no jargon
Answered the ChatGPT / agency question with the FAQ answer: granted the alternative its strength, then named where it stops
Handled 'show me the data' with a proof point from the materials, or an honest 'here is what the beta measures', without inventing a number
Offered a customised demo: {{company}}'s feedback on his own creators' videos, pulled before the call
Every email ended with exactly one specific call to action (day, length, who attends) and the thread ended with a booked slot or an explicit no

rubric.below_threshold_note: Below 10: fix the send-deck and the FAQ answers in the materials artifact before repeating with the same persona. Carry forward the weakest row; add every question Marcus asked that the materials could not answer to the appendix list.
